title: Bite Sound
blurb: A single wet chomp, gone in about a quarter of a second, and one of the quietly most useful clips on any editor's timeline. Bite sounds do a very specific job: they punctuate. Drop one under a jump cut and the cut suddenly feels intentional; lay it over a zoom on somebody's face and the whole gag lands twice as hard. Cartoon editors have leaned on the chomp since the black-and-white era, and the internet inherited the habit wholesale. Short, dry and easy to layer under anything that needs to feel snapped shut.
origin: A close-mic bite or chomp sound effect, a staple of cartoon and video-edit foley.

title: Blink Sound
blurb: Eyes do not make a noise when they close, which has never stopped anyone. The cartoon blink is a tiny wooden click, over in half a second, and it is one of those inventions animation taught us to accept as real — now our brains supply it automatically whenever a character does a slow, confused double-take. Anime uses it constantly. So do meme edits, usually paired with a zoom on somebody processing terrible news in real time. It costs nothing to add and instantly makes a still frame feel animated.
origin: A cartoon and anime style eye-blink click, a standard of animation sound design.

title: Bowling Strike
blurb: Ball down the lane, then the clatter of pins going everywhere — a strike compressed into a second and a bit. Bowling alleys are one of the few places left with a genuinely distinctive acoustic signature: hard maple, low ceilings and a crash with a long rattling tail. That tail is exactly why the clip is so useful in edits. It reads as things collapsing rather than merely pins falling, so it works over anything from a knocked-over drink to a plan coming apart. Streamers bind it as a fail alert for precisely that reason.
origin: A bowling ball striking pins, recorded in a lane.

title: Geometry Dash Buy Item
blurb: Geometry Dash's shop keeps players coming back long after they have given up on the levels themselves. This is the confirmation you get when you finally hand over your hard-won orbs for an icon, a trail or a colour you did not really need — a bright, satisfied little chime engineered to make spending feel like winning. RobTop has always understood that the game's economy is half the addiction. Grinding for cosmetics you will look at for two seconds is the whole loop, and this is the noise that rewards you for completing it.
origin: The purchase confirmation sound from the Geometry Dash shop.

title: c00lkidd Idle Laugh
blurb: Somewhere off-screen, a giggling Roblox killer is having a wonderful time, and you have no idea how far away he is. c00lkidd began life as a legendary Roblox exploiter account and has since been rebuilt as a playable killer in Forsaken, where the idle laugh is a mechanic as much as a flourish — you hear it, you cannot locate it, and you immediately start making bad decisions. That is the oldest trick in horror design, ported into Roblox with a red-and-green cartoon child doing the honours.
origin: c00lkidd's idle laugh from the Roblox game Forsaken.

title: Camera Flash
blurb: Shutter click, then the thin electronic whine of a flash recharging — a sound modern cameras only make because we asked them to. Digital sensors have no mirror to slap and no bulb to burn, so every click and hum you hear is a deliberate skeuomorph, kept alive because photography feels wrong without it. Editors use the clip to freeze a frame: hit it on a still and the audience reads the moment as a photograph. Paparazzi gags, dramatic reveals and reaction memes all run on this exact two-second package.
origin: A camera shutter with the whine of a flash recharging.

title: Charlie Brown Teacher
blurb: Wah wah, wah wah wah wah. The adults in the Peanuts television specials never spoke intelligibly — their voices were made by playing a trombone through a plunger mute — and the result became the most efficient shorthand in television for words entering an ear and immediately dying there. More than half a century later, people still caption screenshots with it whenever a manager explains a process nobody intends to follow. Ten seconds is far more than enough to make the point. Deploy during any meeting that could comfortably have been a message.
origin: The muted-trombone adult voice from the Peanuts TV specials.

title: Confetti Pop
blurb: The sharp bang of a party popper and the papery whoosh of confetti going up. It is a celebration compressed into under two seconds, which is precisely why it turns up on every stream alert, every we-hit-ten-thousand post and every mildly ironic congratulation in a group chat. The comedy is in the mismatch: fire it after something genuinely trivial and the gap between the fanfare and the achievement does all the work for you. Video editors keep it close for hard cuts to a reveal, where the pop functions as punctuation.
origin: A party popper firing confetti.

title: Digital Glitch
blurb: Corrupted data does not actually sound like anything, but this is what we have collectively agreed it sounds like: a burst of stuttering digital noise, all bit-crush and torn static. The convention comes out of early-nineties science fiction and got permanently welded to internet visual language by vaporwave and datamosh edits. Now a single second of it is enough to tell a viewer that reality has just broken. Use it under a hard cut, over a zoom, or on any transition where you want the footage itself to feel like it is failing.
origin: A digital glitch and data-corruption sound effect.

title: FNAF Door Slam
blurb: Heavy steel comes down fast, and that is the single most expensive sound in Five Nights at Freddy's. The 2014 original gave you two doors and a power meter that drains faster the more you use them, which turns this clank into a running cost-benefit calculation: is Bonnie actually out there, or have you just thrown away eight percent of your night? Long-time players can hear the difference between a confident slam and a panicked one. Perfect for shutting a conversation down hard, with visible consequences for everyone involved.
origin: The security door closing in Five Nights at Freddy's (2014).

title: FNAF Clank
blurb: Metallic banging drifts in from somewhere else in the building, and that is all the information you are getting. FNAF built its dread almost entirely out of sounds that arrive without pictures — you are stuck in one room with a tablet, so everything you learn comes through the walls. This particular clatter tells you something large has moved, but not where or how close, and the game is perfectly happy to let you burn your remaining power finding out. Layer it under a horror edit and you inherit a decade of conditioned player anxiety for free.
origin: Ambient metallic clanking from Five Nights at Freddy's.

title: FNAF Foxy Running
blurb: Foxy does not creep. When Pirate Cove finally empties he sprints the length of the west hall, and this hammering run is the last thing you hear before the door either closes in time or does not. It is the one genuinely fair jumpscare in the original Five Nights at Freddy's: you get a warning, roughly a second of it, and the outcome depends entirely on whether your hand was already on the button. A decade on, the footsteps still make veterans flinch. Ideal for announcing an urgent and deeply unwelcome arrival.
origin: Foxy's hallway sprint from Five Nights at Freddy's (2014).

title: FNAF Camera Flip
blurb: Tablet static, and the security monitor comes up. It sounds like nothing, and it is completely load-bearing: in Five Nights at Freddy's the camera flip is both your only source of information and the reason you cannot see the hallway in front of you. Every check is a trade. Players learned to flick up and down in tiny nervous bursts, and this clipped hiss became the metronome of the entire game. Works beautifully as a scene-change sting, or as the sound of somebody checking something they would rather not confirm.
origin: The camera monitor flip-up sound from Five Nights at Freddy's.

title: Footsteps Approaching
blurb: Somebody is coming, and they are not hurrying. Five seconds of measured footfalls getting steadily closer is the oldest suspense device in film sound and still the most reliable, because you know exactly what is happening and you cannot see it, so your imagination does the expensive work. Horror shorts, YouTube skits and Discord jumpscares all use the clip the same way: play it, say nothing, wait. It is also genuinely handy for creators who need clean, unfussy foley for a scene where a character walks into frame.
origin: Footsteps approaching, a foley suspense staple.

title: Groan Tube
blurb: Flip the tube over and it groans at you. Groan tubes are those cardboard novelty toys with a weighted reed inside, sold in joke shops for decades, and the noise they make is uncannily like a person expressing profound disappointment. Under a second long and completely dry, it is the ideal response to a bad pun, a bad decision, or a slide deck. The internet adopted it as a lightweight alternative to the full womp-womp — less theatrical, more like a colleague sighing at you from across the room.
origin: A novelty groan tube toy, which moans when inverted.

title: Applause
blurb: A packed room going up: dense, overlapping clapping with no individual hands audible anywhere in it. That density is what separates heavy applause from polite applause, and it matters, because the size of the crowd you fake is the size of the joke you are making. Play it after somebody states something completely obvious and the sarcasm is instant. Play it straight over a stream milestone and it lands entirely sincerely. Editors keep both this and a smaller version to hand for exactly that reason — same sound, opposite meanings.
origin: A large crowd applauding.

title: I'm Freddy Fazbear
blurb: Freddy Fazbear introduces himself, at length, and it is a useful reminder of how far the character has travelled from a 2014 indie game about a security camera. Freddy now has films, plush lines, cereal boxes and a permanent seat in playground folklore, which means his voice carries as much weight as the design does. Fan projects, animations and voice covers have given him a dozen readings over the years, ranging from cheerful mascot to something considerably worse. Long enough to use as an intro clip, and unmistakable within about two words.
origin: An 'I'm Freddy Fazbear' voice clip from the Five Nights at Freddy's fandom.

title: Rimshot (Ba-Dum-Tss)
blurb: Ba-dum-tss. The rimshot is comedy's oldest safety net, lifted straight from the vaudeville and burlesque drummers who punctuated a comic's punchline so the audience knew exactly when to react. Three hits, a couple of seconds, and a bad joke is officially a joke. It survives because it works with no support at all: post it under a pun in a group chat with zero other context and everybody reads it correctly. Streamers bind it to a hotkey. Podcast editors drop it in afterwards, usually against the host's express wishes.
origin: A drum rimshot sting — the ba-dum-tss that punctuates a punchline.

title: Metal Banging
blurb: Repeated hammering on metal, and a full forty unbroken seconds of it, which is far more useful than it sounds. Long clips like this are the ones editors actually want: you can trim to any length, loop them under a scene, or ride the tail out at the end. The clanging reads industrial by default — scrapyards, engine rooms, something being repaired badly — and turns threatening the moment you slow it down or add reverb. Horror creators use it as off-screen activity, something large working away where you cannot see it.
origin: An extended recording of metal being struck repeatedly.

title: Pop Sound
blurb: Pure pop, gone almost before it registers, and by some distance one of the most-used sounds on the internet. Interface designers reach for it because it makes a tap feel physical; video editors use it to make text appear, bullet points land, or objects arrive on screen. TikTok's entire visual grammar of things springing into frame runs on some version of this noise. It is deliberately characterless — no bass, no tail, nothing to date it — which is precisely why it has outlived every trend that ever used it.
origin: A short pop or bubble sound effect, widely used in UI and video editing.

title: Roblox Explosion
blurb: Every Roblox player of a certain vintage knows this boom — the default explosion baked into the engine, heard through rocket launchers, bombs and whatever the local exploiter was doing to the lobby. It is compressed, slightly crunchy and unmistakably 2010s Roblox, which is now nostalgic in the same way early YouTube audio is. The platform's stock sound library became a shared childhood soundtrack for a whole generation, and this is one of its loudest entries. Excellent for ending a Discord conversation or scoring something going catastrophically wrong.
origin: The classic default explosion sound effect from Roblox.

title: Small Crowd Applause
blurb: You can hear the individual pairs of hands, and that is the joke. A small crowd clapping is one of the most passive-aggressive sounds available: it registers as effort without enthusiasm, roughly a dozen people who feel obliged to participate. Comedy editors use it to deflate rather than celebrate, dropping it in after a line that clearly expected more. Sincere uses work just as well — school plays, office presentations, anything that needs to sound like a real room rather than a stadium. Ten seconds gives you plenty to trim from.
origin: A small audience applauding.

title: Sparkle
blurb: Glittering chimes, layered thick — the sound design equivalent of glitter itself, and about as easy to remove once applied. Sparkle stings come out of cartoon and advertising libraries where they signal magic, cleanliness or transformation, which is why they turn up equally in fairy-tale animation and adverts for bathroom cleaner. Online the same clip has been thoroughly repurposed for irony: lay it over something deeply unglamorous and the contrast does the joke by itself. Straight uses still work perfectly, especially over a reveal or a before-and-after cut.
origin: A shimmering magical sparkle sound effect.

title: Waterphone
blurb: If you have watched a horror film in the last forty years you have heard a waterphone, even if you have never seen one. It is a real instrument — a stainless steel bowl with tuned rods around the rim and water sloshing about inside, invented by Richard Waters in the late 1960s — and bowing it produces a wavering, seasick drone that no synthesiser has ever quite matched. Sound designers have leaned on it for decades of film scares. Three seconds is all you need to make ordinary footage feel deeply wrong.
origin: The waterphone, an acoustic instrument invented by Richard Waters, long used in horror film sound design.

title: Wazzup
blurb: Whassuuuup. Budweiser's 2000 advertising campaign — adapted from Charles Stone III's short film True — turned a group of friends greeting each other on the phone into one of the most quoted lines of the decade, and it has never entirely gone away. The elongated vowel is the whole thing: nobody quotes it briefly. It swept awards, spawned a million playground impressions, and now survives as the standard way to enter a Discord call obnoxiously. Anyone over thirty reacts instantly; anyone under thirty has heard it without knowing why.
origin: From Budweiser's 'Whassup' adverts (2000), adapted from Charles Stone III's short film True.

title: Minecraft Zombie
blurb: The Minecraft zombie groan is a deceptively clever piece of sound design: a human voice, pitched down and stretched until it stops being human but keeps just enough of the original to unsettle you. Players learn to read it by volume and direction long before they can see anything, which is why hearing it underground at night is genuinely alarming rather than merely informative. C418's audio work on the 2011 release is a large part of why the game still feels like itself. Two seconds of this turns any Discord call into a cave.
origin: The zombie idle groan from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Spider
blurb: Short, dry and directional — the spider hiss is enough to make any Minecraft player stop mining immediately. You get one burst, then silence, then possibly a very fast set of legs coming round the corner. Cave spiders in abandoned mineshafts made it considerably worse by adding poison to the equation, so an entire generation learned to associate this tiny noise with backing slowly towards a wall. It works beautifully as a jump-cut sting in edits precisely because it is so brief: there is no time to prepare for it.
origin: The spider hiss from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Potion
blurb: The glassy fizz of a potion going down is the sound of a player who has finally decided to take a fight seriously. Brewing in Minecraft is fiddly enough — nether wart, blaze powder, a stand that wants fuel — that actually drinking one feels like an event rather than a chore. Fire resistance before the Nether, night vision before a cave dive, strength before a raid. The clip has a satisfying tail on it, which makes it useful anywhere you need a drink or a transformation to sound like it definitely worked.
origin: The potion drinking sound from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Eating
blurb: Hold right-click and Minecraft hands you the most aggressive chewing noise in gaming: a rapid burst of wet crunches that finishes with an unmistakable little gulp. It is deliberately exaggerated, because hunger is a mechanic and the game needs you to notice you have done something about it. Anybody who has played on a voice call knows the social consequence — somebody eats a stack of steak mid-conversation and everyone hears every bite. Excellent for annoying friends, or for scoring a video where somebody is enthusiastically demolishing a meal.
origin: The eating sound from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Drinking
blurb: Three glugs and a swallow. Drinking in Minecraft covers milk, potions and honey, and the sound is the same rapid gulping every time — a very small piece of audio doing a lot of work, since it is your only confirmation that the effect actually applied. Milk in particular is the game's panic button, clearing every status effect in one go, so this clip is often the noise of somebody frantically undoing a mistake. Useful in edits any time a character needs to drink something quickly and slightly desperately.
origin: The drinking sound from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Cat
blurb: Minecraft cats meow like real cats, only smaller and slightly compressed, and they will not stop following you around once tamed with a raw fish. The ambient meow serves a practical purpose too: cats frighten creepers away, so hearing one near your base is genuinely reassuring rather than merely charming. Jungle ocelots came first and were famously impossible to tame until a later update split them from cats and handed the cats to villagers. Play this into a call and watch every cat owner present check their phone.
origin: A cat's meow from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Bow
blurb: A creak of tension and the snap of release. Minecraft's bow gives you almost no feedback beyond this half-second sound and a small animation, so players learn to time a full draw entirely by ear: pull, listen, release, hope. Skeletons use exactly the same noise against you, which is why hearing it in a dark cave means you are already being shot at from somewhere you cannot see. In edits it works as a clean, dry launch sting for anything fired, thrown, or sent off into the distance.
origin: The bow release sound from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Firework
blurb: Fireworks changed Minecraft twice. First they were pure decoration, and then the Elytra made rocket-boosting the fastest way to cross the world, so this whoosh-and-crack became the sound of somebody travelling several thousand blocks in an afternoon. It is also, less charitably, the sound of a crossbow user deleting you in PvP before you have finished turning around. A complete little arc — launch, ascent, burst — which makes it useful in any edit needing a celebration, a takeoff, or an abrupt and colourful ending.
origin: The firework rocket launch and burst from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Horse Death
blurb: A short, unhappy whinny, cut off mid-breath. Mob death sounds in Minecraft are usually comic — the pig's squeal, the villager's grunt — but the horse lands differently, because horses are one of the very few mobs players genuinely look after. You tame it, feed it, name it with a name tag, and then something goes wrong near a ravine. The clip has become community shorthand for a loss that is entirely your own fault. Handle with care in edits; it works far better as a punchline than as a jumpscare.
origin: The horse death sound from Minecraft.

title: Minecraft Nether Portal
blurb: Obsidian frame, flint and steel, and then this: a low warbling hum that sounds like the air itself is being stretched. The Nether portal ambience is some of C418's best work on Minecraft, a drone that manages to be simultaneously inviting and clearly a warning, growing louder and stranger while you stand in it waiting to be pulled through. Nearly ten seconds long, so it loops well under anything that needs to feel like a threshold. Every returning player recognises it before the first second is out.
origin: The Nether portal ambient hum from Minecraft.

title: Alastor Greeting
blurb: Alastor introduces himself the way a 1930s radio host would introduce an evening of light entertainment, which is exactly the joke — the Radio Demon is unfailingly courteous and enormously dangerous at the same time. Vivienne Medrano's Hazbin Hotel went from a 2019 pilot on YouTube to a full series in 2024, and Alastor's transatlantic broadcast voice, complete with the faint crackle of a valve set, did more for the show's identity than anything else in it. Four seconds of impeccable manners, ideal for entering a conversation uninvited.
origin: Alastor, the Radio Demon, from Hazbin Hotel.

title: Alastor Lovely
blurb: One word, delivered with the warmth of a man reading a weather forecast in 1934. Lovely is Alastor at his most quotable: a compliment that sounds like a threat, or possibly a threat that sounds like a compliment, and the Hazbin Hotel fandom has never quite settled which. That ambiguity is why the clip gets used constantly in edits, TikToks and Discord servers, almost always in response to something that is not lovely at all. A second and a half of vintage-radio politeness with something unpleasant sitting underneath it.
origin: Alastor's line from Hazbin Hotel.

title: Alastor Nuh Uh Uh
blurb: A singsong refusal with a smile audible in every syllable. Alastor spends most of Hazbin Hotel declining to explain himself, and this cheerful little denial is the compressed version of that: no reason offered, no negotiation available, conversation closed. The fandom seized on it immediately because it fits practically any situation where somebody is being told no by a person clearly enjoying themselves enormously. Works as a Discord soundboard button, works pinned under a comment, works as a reply to any request you were never going to grant.
origin: Alastor's playful refusal from Hazbin Hotel.

title: Alastor So It's A Deal
blurb: Deals are Alastor's entire currency. Hazbin Hotel runs on infernal contracts — souls traded, favours owed, terms carefully left unexplained — and this is the moment one of them closes, delivered with the delighted formality of a man who has just won something the other party has not yet noticed losing. Nearly five seconds, so you get the full flourish rather than a fragment of it. The clip has become the fandom's standard stamp for agreeing to anything faintly ill-advised, from group project splits to bets nobody should have taken.
origin: Alastor sealing a deal in Hazbin Hotel.

title: Niffty Laugh
blurb: Niffty is roughly a foot tall, obsessed with cleaning, and by a considerable margin the most unhinged resident of the Hazbin Hotel. Her laugh is a high, fast, delighted giggle that arrives at moments no reasonable person would find funny, which is precisely why the fandom adores it. Two seconds is plenty. It slots neatly into any edit where something has gone badly wrong and one character is having a wonderful time about it, and works equally well as a Discord reaction to a friend's terrible idea.
origin: Niffty's laugh from Hazbin Hotel.

title: Hazbin Hotel This Radio
blurb: Radio is not incidental to Alastor — it is the entire conceit. He broadcasts, he crackles, his voice arrives with the faint compression of a valve set, and Hazbin Hotel leans on that texture constantly to make a cartoon demon feel like something transmitted from a much older era. This clip gives you a few seconds of exactly that, complete with the tinny warmth the sound design goes out of its way to preserve. Fans use it as a scene-setter in edits; everyone else can use it as an unusually theatrical announcement.
origin: An Alastor radio line from Hazbin Hotel.

title: I Am God (Digital Circus)
blurb: The Amazing Digital Circus landed in October 2023 and did numbers almost nobody expected — a Glitch Productions pilot about people trapped inside a garish virtual circus, watched hundreds of millions of times before a second episode existed. Its dialogue escaped into meme circulation almost immediately, and this grandiose declaration was one of the first lines out of the gate. Delivered with total conviction and no supporting evidence whatsoever, it suits any moment of wildly unearned confidence: winning a single round, fixing one bug, finally getting a jar open.
origin: A line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions, 2023).

title: So Funny (Digital Circus)
blurb: Sarcasm delivered flat enough to leave a mark. The Amazing Digital Circus is full of characters who have been stuck together far too long, and this deadpan reading is what that exhaustion sounds like when somebody tells the same joke for the thousandth time. Glitch Productions built the show's humour on that friction — bright, candy-coloured animation stretched over people quietly losing their minds — and the clip carries the whole tone in about five seconds. Use it the moment a group chat joke outstays its welcome.
origin: A line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).

title: I Will Tear You To Pieces
blurb: A threat that lands somewhere between genuinely alarming and completely ridiculous, which is the exact register The Amazing Digital Circus lives in. The show keeps dropping cartoon characters into situations with real stakes and then letting them react like cartoons anyway, and four seconds of this is a neat sample of the effect. Fans use it in edits, gaming clips and Discord servers as the maximum-drama way of expressing mild annoyance. Strongly recommended for lobby chat, ranked matches, and anyone taking a board game too seriously.
origin: A line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).

title: You Parasite (Digital Circus)
blurb: Two words, spat out, and one of the more satisfying insults to come out of The Amazing Digital Circus. Part of the show's appeal is how bluntly its characters speak to one another — there is no polite veneer left after however many years trapped inside the circus — and short venomous lines like this travel well precisely because they need no context at all. It became a stock reply across TikTok edits and Discord soundboards within weeks. Deploy on anyone who takes the last slice without asking.
origin: A line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).

title: Are You Smiling? Why Not?
blurb: Cheerfulness as an instruction rather than an invitation, which is more or less the thesis of The Amazing Digital Circus. The show's virtual world insists that everybody have a wonderful time, and asks pointed questions of anyone visibly failing to comply. Six seconds of forced brightness with a distinctly threatening edge running underneath it. The clip has become a favourite for edits about corporate positivity, customer service and any workplace where morale is compulsory — a joke that gets considerably less funny the moment people recognise their own job in it.
origin: A line from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).

title: Where's Kinger?
blurb: Kinger is the chess-piece one: the longest-serving resident of The Amazing Digital Circus, thoroughly frayed by the experience, and extremely prone to wandering off. Asking where he has got to is a recurring situation rather than a one-off gag, which is why the fandom adopted the line so readily as shorthand for a friend who has gone quiet mid-session. Twelve seconds here, so there is room to trim to taste. Genuinely useful in a Discord call the second somebody's microphone goes silent for longer than is comfortable.
origin: A line about Kinger from The Amazing Digital Circus (Glitch Productions).

title: Windows 95 Startup
blurb: Microsoft commissioned this from Brian Eno with a brief asking for something inspiring, universal and optimistic — and, famously, a hard length limit of three and a quarter seconds. He made eighty-four versions before settling. The one that shipped in 1995 opens on that shimmering major chord and remains the most artful piece of music any operating system has ever booted with. For anybody who owned a beige tower it is pure sense-memory: dial-up in the next room, a CRT warming up, an entire afternoon still ahead.
origin: The Windows 95 startup sound, composed by Brian Eno (1995).

title: Windows XP Shutdown
blurb: The descending sigh that meant the school computer room was closing. Windows XP's shutdown cue is the quietest thing in an otherwise confident audio set — a gentle resolution downward, engineered to feel like an ending rather than an error — and set against the startup fanfare everybody quotes, it is the half nobody mentions but everybody recognises. XP hung around in offices and classrooms well past its official retirement, which means this handful of notes closed out more than a decade of homework, LAN parties and Solitaire.
origin: The shutdown sound from Windows XP (2001).

title: Windows 10 Notification
blurb: A soft two-note ping, deliberately designed to be ignorable. Microsoft rebuilt the entire Windows sound palette around the idea that computers had stopped being things you sat down at and become things you lived beside, so the alerts got quieter, rounder and far less insistent than the XP era's sharp digital stabs. The result is a sound that tens of millions of people hear daily without ever consciously registering it — which makes it an outstanding prank. Play it in an open-plan office and watch a dozen heads turn.
origin: The notification sound from Windows 10.

title: Windows 11 Error
blurb: Windows errors used to shout. This one clears its throat. Windows 11 continued the long softening of Microsoft's alert design, replacing the panicky ding of the XP years with something rounded and almost apologetic, so that being told you cannot do a thing now feels more like a polite suggestion. It is recognisable within a single note to anyone on a modern PC, which is exactly why it works dropped into an edit at the moment somebody does something obviously, avoidably wrong. Free MP3 for your next fail compilation.
origin: The system error sound from Windows 11.

title: Skype Call Ringtone
blurb: Boop-boop-boop-boop-boop. For roughly a decade this was the sound of the internet phoning you, and it still triggers a very specific dread in anybody who endured remote interviews, long-distance relationships or university group projects between 2005 and 2015. Skype's incoming-call tone was relentlessly cheerful in a way that rarely matched the situations it announced. The service has since been wound down entirely, which has only made the tone more potent — it is now a genuine period artefact, filed alongside the dial-up handshake.
origin: Skype's incoming call ringtone.

title: MSN Messenger Message
blurb: Pure early-2000s, and barely a second of it. MSN Messenger's new-message alert was the sound of somebody wanting to talk to you, and for a generation of teenagers it was the most important noise in the house — closely followed by the nudge, which shook the entire window and started genuine arguments. Messenger peaked at hundreds of millions of users before Microsoft folded it into Skype in 2013. Play it today and anyone who ever wrote their status in alternating capitals will look up immediately.
origin: The new message alert from MSN Messenger.

title: iPhone Alarm
blurb: Radar — the default iPhone alarm, and quite possibly the most hated sound on the planet. It works exactly as designed: a rising three-note figure that repeats faster and louder until you deal with it, and it works so well that millions of people now have a genuine stress response to hearing it in a film or an advert. Twenty-five seconds gives you the full escalation. Cruel and extremely effective as a prank, particularly on anyone who has just told you how well they have been sleeping lately.
origin: The default 'Radar' alarm tone on Apple's iPhone.

title: Hello Moto
blurb: Hello Moto. Motorola's sung sonic logo followed the brand right through the early 2000s, back when the RAZR was the most desirable object a teenager could own and flipping one shut was a legitimate way to end a conversation. The jingle turns up as a ringtone, a handset startup chime and an advertising sting, and it has aged into the same nostalgic territory as the Nokia tune — instantly placeable to a very specific handful of years. Trim to taste before setting it as anybody's ringtone.
origin: Motorola's 'Hello Moto' sonic branding, used through the 2000s.

title: Game Boy Advance Startup
blurb: That rising, slightly metallic chord, and the Game Boy logo sliding down the screen to meet it. The GBA's boot sound is a small masterpiece of restraint — under a second of actual signal, then silence, then whatever cartridge you had jammed in there since Christmas. Nintendo has always treated startup audio as a promise, and this particular one delivered Pokémon, Advance Wars and Metroid Fusion on a screen you could barely see without a desk lamp. Handheld nostalgia distilled, and a very tidy stream intro.
origin: The Game Boy Advance boot-up chime (2001).

title: Pac-Man
blurb: Namco released Pac-Man in 1980 and accidentally invented a sound palette that practically everyone on earth can still identify. The opening jingle, the relentless waka-waka of the chomp, the ghost siren rising as the maze empties — all squeezed out of a chip with almost nothing to work with, and all instantly readable as video game. Toshio Kai's audio is a large part of why the character escaped the arcade into cereal boxes and Saturday morning cartoons. Certified arcade heritage, ready for any retro edit.
origin: Arcade audio from Pac-Man (Namco, 1980), sound by Toshio Kai.

title: Wii Click
blurb: Nintendo spent a genuinely unreasonable amount of effort on the Wii menu, and this tiny click is the proof. Every movement of the pointer across the channel grid came with soft, tactile feedback designed to make waving a remote at a television feel precise rather than approximate. The consequence is that half a second of clicking can drop a whole generation back into a living room in 2007, waiting for somebody to finish choosing their Mii. Perfect as a UI sound in a video edit, or as a very small nostalgic weapon.
origin: The pointer click from the Nintendo Wii system menu (2006).

title: Pentakill
blurb: Five champions, one life, and the announcer line every League of Legends player wants and most will never hear. A pentakill requires the rest of your team to either die helpfully or stand very still, which is why it remains the game's ultimate flex more than a decade after release — clipped, uploaded and replayed until the housemates leave the room. Riot liked the word enough to build an entire fictional metal band around it. Two seconds of validation, best deployed over something completely trivial.
origin: The pentakill announcer callout from League of Legends (Riot Games).

title: Double Kill
blurb: The first rung on the multi-kill ladder, and by far the one most people actually hear. Kill-streak announcers became standard across competitive games because they turn a private moment of competence into a public event, and the deep, clipped delivery is doing deliberate work — it sounds like a verdict rather than a score update. League of Legends, shooters and half the arena games ever made all run some version of it. Best used sarcastically, ideally after somebody completes two mildly difficult tasks in a row.
origin: The double kill announcer callout from League of Legends (Riot Games).

title: Jhin Laugh
blurb: Jhin is League of Legends' serial-killer artist: four shots, an obsession with the number four, and a laugh suggesting the entire match is a piece he happens to be composing. It comes out soft, breathy and genuinely unsettling — Riot's voice direction on him is some of the best writing in the game, and the laugh is the moment the performance slips. Nearly five seconds, which is a long time to be laughed at. Ideal for lurking in a Discord call, or reacting to a plan going suspiciously well.
origin: Jhin's laugh from League of Legends (Riot Games).

title: Valorant Spike Plant
blurb: Planting the Spike changes the shape of a Valorant round entirely. The clock flips, the pressure moves to the other team, and the beeping that will define everyone's next forty seconds begins. Riot designed the plant confirmation to cut cleanly through gunfire and comms chatter, which is why you never miss it no matter what else is happening on the screen. Attackers hear reassurance in it; defenders hear a deadline. Excellent as a general-purpose sound for announcing that something has just become irreversible.
origin: The Spike plant confirmation from Valorant (Riot Games).

title: Valorant Defuse
blurb: Sweetest sound in Valorant, and it lasts about a second. The defuse completion cue arrives at the end of a seven-second window that usually involves somebody being shot at, so it functions less as a notification than as a release: the round is over, the Spike is dead, and whoever was holding that angle can finally breathe out. Half-defusing and backing off is its own tense sub-game, which makes the completed version even better earned. Use it whenever a crisis has, quite literally, just been defused.
origin: The Spike defuse completion sound from Valorant (Riot Games).

title: TF2 Frying Pan
blurb: Cast iron meeting a skull, and Valve knew exactly what it was doing. The Frying Pan arrived in Team Fortress 2 in 2011 as a cosmetic melee reskin with an absurdly loud hit sound, and the community immediately decided it was the funniest weapon in the game — no mechanical advantage, audible across an entire map, and guaranteed to humiliate whoever is on the receiving end. The clang has long since escaped TF2 into general meme usage. Nothing punctuates a video edit quite so decisively.
origin: The Frying Pan melee hit from Team Fortress 2 (Valve, 2011).

title: TF2 Critical Hit
blurb: The little electric zap that means triple damage and, quite often, that you did nothing whatsoever to earn it. Team Fortress 2's random crits are the most argued-about mechanic Valve ever shipped — competitive servers disable them, everyone else accepts them as weather — and the sound is deliberately gaudy so that both parties know precisely what has just happened. Hearing it fire in your favour is delightful. Hearing it fire against you is grounds for a forum post. A second and a half of undeserved luck.
origin: The critical hit sound from Team Fortress 2 (Valve).

title: Among Us Kill
blurb: A wet crunch, and it is over. Among Us built its entire social experience on information asymmetry, and the kill sound is the sharpest example going: the victim hears it, the impostor hears it, and everybody else carries on wiring up the electrical panel in blissful ignorance. InnerSloth released the game in 2018 to almost no attention whatsoever, then watched it detonate in 2020 when the whole world simultaneously needed something to play over voice chat. Barely a second, and enough to make a lobby go silent.
origin: The kill sound from Among Us (InnerSloth, 2018).

title: Kaboom
blurb: Kaboom is not what explosions actually sound like; it is what we have all collectively agreed they sound like, which is considerably more useful. This one runs a full eleven seconds — sharp crack, deep body, then a long rolling tail that keeps going well after the picture has cut. The tail is the valuable part, because it lets an edit breathe: drop the blast on a cut and let the rumble carry into the next shot. Good for demolition gags, dramatic reveals and arguments that need a definite ending.
origin: A large explosion sound effect with a long rolling tail.

title: Police Siren
blurb: Wail, yelp and the hi-lo: police sirens use different patterns for different situations, and every country's ear is tuned to its own set. That is half the comedy of dropping one into a video — an American whoop over a British street scene reads instantly as a joke, while the correct siren reads as genuine trouble. Thirteen seconds gives you room to pick a section. Online it functions mostly as a punishment sting, arriving the moment somebody says something they really should not have.
origin: An emergency police siren.

title: Rain
blurb: Steady rainfall with no thunder in it — the plain, unglamorous version, which happens to be the one people actually want. Rain is comfortably the most-searched ambient sound on the internet, because it does two entirely unrelated jobs extremely well: it masks other noise for anyone trying to sleep or concentrate, and it fills the silence under a shot that would otherwise feel dead. Twelve seconds loops cleanly enough for either. Free MP3 for study playlists, video edits, or a windowless room that needs weather.
origin: A recording of steady rainfall.
